Title: The Trial of Avaiki
Pitch_Text:
Trapped in Avaiki, the primordial cave, face the other deities by creating hybrids that will populate the new world.

Trial of Avaiki is a competitive multiplayer deck-building game in which players build their deck by buying and merging cards before facing each other in turn-based battles.
SumUp_Text:
Trial of Avaiki is my first large-scale project developed outside of my academic studies. It brought many challenges, such as organization and remote collaboration.
It is also the first project on which I was not the only programmer.

This project also allowed me to discover multiplayer management, notably through Netcode for GameObjects as well as the Lobby and Relay services.

However, it is important to note that this project could not be completed due to a lack of time near the end of development.
Realisation_Text:
During this project, I took on the role of lead programmer to coordinate task breakdowns. Here are my main contributions:

• Small team management: At the start of the project, we were four motivated programmers. The team size led me to set up several organizational tools, such as schedules and a task management system. However, several members quickly dropped out, leaving a much smaller team than originally planned. This forced me to rework part of the organization and development priorities, as we were no longer able to achieve all initial goals.

• Multiplayer system: I handled the integration of multiplayer features. Due to the competitive nature of the game, it was necessary to implement a more secure and robust server-authoritative architecture to prevent cheating. However, because of the constraints mentioned earlier, some aspects of multiplayer, such as peer-to-peer and lobby creation, could only be prototyped and were not included in the final version.

• Gameplay programming: The card structure and the combat system formed the core of the gameplay. The goal was to design a system as modular as possible to allow fast addition and modification of effects and cards. We therefore chose an inheritance-based class architecture for both effects and cards. By assigning specific IDs to each effect, it became easy to trigger them from anywhere using a simple function call.

• Tooling: Early in the project, while the concept was still evolving, I developed a custom in-game console to facilitate debugging directly in builds. This console allowed us to retrieve logs and, more importantly, to call internal script functions through simple commands. It proved to be a major time-saver, especially during multiplayer implementation.
Amelioration_Text:
To address team dropouts, we repeatedly tried to onboard new members during production. However, this onboarding process was not well managed, and it was difficult to efficiently communicate the current state of the project so new members could get up to speed quickly.
Although inheritance-based architecture was a clear improvement over my previous projects, using interfaces would have been more beneficial to make the system even more modular and easier to adapt.
Multiplayer management was sometimes very difficult, and we often made certain systems unnecessarily complex, mainly due to our initial lack of experience.

However, this project allowed me to gain hands-on experience with multiplayer systems while learning the basics of team-based programming.
